title: Why 'You Can See Everything' is captivating audiences
summary: Jeffrey Brown looks at Nathan Fielder's unconventional documentary about Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes, which has sold out screenings and won a wider release. New York Times critic Alissa Wilkinson explains that the film draws on Holmes's notoriety and Fielder's fan base, and argues it deliberately tests how audiences decide what to believe on screen. Investigative reporter John Carreyrou counters that the film risks making Holmes sympathetic while she still sidesteps responsibility for the fraud.
focus: Shadow Wilkinson's answer on how her own view of Holmes shifted while watching, and her closing point that every documentary shapes reality, this one just pushes it further — both are measured, clearly paced analytical speech.

vocab.meaning: to praise or promote something or someone loudly and insistently
vocab.context: Used to describe how Holmes was once promoted as a brilliant young billionaire before Theranos collapsed.
vocab.example: The vendor touted its platform as a turnkey solution, but the pilot exposed major integration gaps.

vocab.meaning: a young person with exceptional talent or ability
vocab.context: Holmes was presented to the public as a youthful genius of Silicon Valley.
vocab.example: The board was so dazzled by the founder's image as a prodigy that nobody asked for audited numbers.

vocab.meaning: deliberately expressionless, especially when being funny
vocab.zh: 面无表情的；冷面幽默的
vocab.context: Describes Fielder's flat, awkward on-screen style that makes his work feel both comic and unsettling.
vocab.example: Her deadpan reply that the forecast was 'aspirational' got the biggest laugh of the steering committee.

vocab.context: Used informally to capture how strange and audacious many viewers found the film.
vocab.example: Quoting a three-week turnaround for a full ERP migration is frankly bonkers.

vocab.meaning: intended or likely to cause strong thought, debate or reaction
vocab.context: The film is framed as one designed to unsettle audiences and spark argument.
vocab.example: We opened the workshop with a deliberately provocative hypothesis: the core business has three years left.

vocab.meaning: a film or programme that mixes real events with dramatised scenes
vocab.context: Fielder's earlier work is described as blending documentary and staged elements in this way.
vocab.example: The client's onboarding video felt less like training and more like a docudrama about the founding team.

vocab.meaning: to break apart or collapse gradually
vocab.context: Refers to the way Theranos fell apart once its technology claims were exposed.
vocab.example: Once the anchor customer walked away, the whole revenue case began to crumble.

vocab.meaning: to illegally obtain money or property from someone by deception
vocab.context: Used when recalling the charges that Holmes cheated investors with false claims.
vocab.example: Misstating pipeline numbers to raise capital isn't optimism — it can amount to defrauding investors.

vocab.meaning: the way someone understands or interprets something
vocab.context: The critic describes how her view of Holmes changed over the course of the film.
vocab.example: Market perception of the brand lagged two years behind the actual product improvements.

vocab.meaning: controlling or influencing people cleverly and unfairly
vocab.zh: 操纵他人的；工于心计的
vocab.context: The investigative reporter argues Holmes's bid for viewers' sympathy is a calculated tactic.
vocab.example: Anchoring the negotiation with a fake competing bid felt manipulative and damaged trust.

vocab.meaning: to make someone seem more ordinary, relatable or sympathetic
vocab.zh: 使人性化；使显得有人情味
vocab.context: A concern is raised that the film makes Holmes too relatable given what she did.
vocab.example: Featuring frontline employees in the annual report helped humanise a fairly faceless utility.

vocab.meaning: new and unusual in an interesting way
vocab.context: The critic describes watching the film as an unfamiliar kind of viewing experience.
vocab.example: The pricing model is novel for the sector, which is both its appeal and its risk.

vocab.meaning: extremely high; far beyond the normal range
vocab.context: Used to stress how extraordinary the interest or audacity around the film was.
vocab.example: Customer churn in the pilot region was off-the-charts, so we paused the rollout.

vocab.meaning: to avoid dealing with a problem or responsibility
vocab.context: Captures the reporter's view that Holmes still avoids owning her wrongdoing and quietly shifts blame.
vocab.example: The CFO sidestepped every question about the write-down during the analyst call.

phrases.meaning: to be too unusual to fit neatly into any type or genre
phrases.context: The film is described as something that doesn't fit the usual documentary or comedy labels.
phrases.example: The startup's business model defies categorisation — part marketplace, part bank, part software vendor.

phrases.context: The critic wonders whether viewers, herself included, are being fooled by what they see on screen.
phrases.example: Several seasoned investors were taken in by the slick demo and never asked to see the backend.

phrases.meaning: to repeatedly doubt one's own judgment or decisions
phrases.context: Describes how the film leaves the audience constantly doubting their own reading of Holmes.
phrases.example: Once the partner challenged the market sizing, the whole team started second-guessing itself.

phrases.meaning: originally; at the very beginning (often used to question why something started)
phrases.context: Used when discussing why the subject agreed to take part in the film at all.
phrases.example: Before we optimise this process, we should ask why the client needs it in the first place.

phrases.meaning: to take something to its most extreme point
phrases.context: The critic argues the film does what all documentaries do in shaping reality, only to an extreme degree.
phrases.example: The cost programme pushed lean staffing to the limit, and service levels finally cracked.
